math.title: Applied letters — discrete population, GDP per capita, and a continuous neighbour
math.context: Denote by $f(t)$ the population of a country (in millions of inhabitants) after $t$ years, where $f(0)$ is the current population. The current population is $12$ millions and it is assumed that it grows by $1.8\%$ per year. After $6$ years the annual growth rate slows to $1\%$ per year. A neighbouring country follows the continuous model $N(t)=9\cdot 10^{6} e^{0.015 t}$. The figure shows the piecewise home-country path. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: It holds that $f(t)=12\cdot 1.018^{t}$ for $0\le t\le 6$.
After $20$ years of uninterrupted $1.8\%$ growth, the population will have grown by more than $45\%$.
The head economist predicts that GDP grows by $4\%$ per year. Then GDP per capita grows by more than $3\%$ per year.
Under the slowdown to $1\%$ after year $6$, the population of $15$ millions is attained at $t>16$.
The neighbouring country's continuous model has a growth rate strictly smaller than $1.5\%$ per year.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Annual growth of $1.8\%$ multiplies the population by the fixed factor $1.018$ each year. Starting from the present level of $12$ million, the closed form is therefore

$$f(t) = 12\cdot 1.018^{t}$$

At $t=0$ this recovers the stated initial population:

$$f(0)=12\cdot 1.018^{0}$$

$$f(0)=12\cdot 1.1$$

$$12\cdot \frac{11}{10}=\frac{66}{5}$$

$$
f(0)=\frac{66}{5} = 12
$$

and each additional year multiplies by one more factor of $1.018$. The displayed formula is exactly the discrete exponential growth model for this country.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Under uninterrupted $1.8\%$ annual growth the population after twenty years is

$$f(20)=12\cdot 1.018^{20}$$

$$f(20)=12\cdot 1.12748236216396078174437376$$

$$12\cdot \frac{107525097099681928801}{95367431640625000000}=\frac{322575291299045786403}{23841857910156250000}$$

$$f(20)=\frac{322575291299045786403}{23841857910156250000}$$

The multiplicative factor and the relative growth are

$$1.018^{20}\approx1.428748\qquad \frac{f(20)-f(0)}{f(0)}=1.018^{20}-1$$

$$1.018^{20}\approx1.428748\qquad \frac{f(20)-f(0)}{f(0)}=1.12748236216396078174437376-1$$

$$\approx 0.428748$$

Converting to a percentage,

$$0.428748\times 100\%\approx42.87\%$$

Compare with the claimed threshold of $45\%$:

$$42.87\% < 45\%$$

Twenty years of $1.8\%$ compounding produce roughly $42.87\%$ net growth, which fails to clear $45\%$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

GDP per capita is the ratio of aggregate GDP to population. If GDP multiplies by $1.04$ each year while population multiplies by $1.018$, the per-capita annual growth factor is the quotient of those bases:

$$\frac{1.04}{1.018}\approx 1.021611$$

Hence the exact annual growth rate of GDP per capita is

$$\frac{1.04}{1.018}-1\approx0.021611\approx2.16\%$$

A linear approximation $0.04-0.018=0.022$ already suggests about $2.2\%$, well below $3\%$. The exact comparison against the claimed bound is

$$0.021611<0.03$$

GDP per capita therefore grows by roughly $2.16\%$ per year, not by more than $3\%$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

For the first six years the population follows $f(t)=12\cdot 1.018^{t}$. At the switch,

$$f(6)=12\cdot 1.018^{6}$$

$$f(6)=12\cdot 1.34012224$$

$$12\cdot \frac{2093941}{1562500}=\frac{6281823}{390625}$$

$$f(6)=\frac{6281823}{390625}$$

$$\approx 13.355739$$

Thereafter the annual base is $1.01$, so for $t>6$

$$f(t) = f(6)\cdot 1.01^{t-6}$$

$$\approx 13.355739\cdot 1.01^{t-6}$$

Reach $15$ million by solving $f(t)=15$:

$$13.355739\cdot 1.01^{t-6} = 15$$

$$1.01^{t-6} = \frac{15}{13.355739}$$

$$\approx 1.123113$$

Take natural logs and isolate $t$:

$$t-6 = \frac{\ln(1.123113)}{\ln 1.01}$$

$$\approx 11.668360$$

$$t_{\mathrm{hit}}\approx17.668360$$

Compare with sixteen years:

$$17.668360>16$$

The $15$-million level is therefore attained strictly after $t=16$, which is the same as $t>16$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The neighbouring population is written in continuous form

$$N(t)=9\cdot 10^{6}\,e^{0.015 t}$$

$$N(t)=9\cdot 1000000\,e^{0.015 t}$$

The coefficient of $t$ in the exponent is the continuous force of growth:

$$
k = 0.015 = 1.5\%
$$

That force is equal to $1.5\%$ per year, not strictly smaller. The corresponding effective annual rate is even larger:

$$e^{0.015}-1\approx0.015113\approx1.511\%$$

$$0.015113>0.015$$

Whether one reads the continuous force or the effective annual rate, the growth is not smaller than $1.5\%$ per year.

So the statement is False.
math.solution_overview:
Annual compounding at $1.8\%$ starts from $12$ million inhabitants:

$$f(t)=12\cdot 1.018^{t}\qquad(0\le t\le 6)$$

After the kink the base drops to $1.01$. At the switch one has $f(6)\approx13.3557$, and the $15$-million hit finishes at $t_{\mathrm{hit}}\approx17.6684$. Over twenty years of uninterrupted $1.8\%$ growth the multiplicative factor is $1.018^{20}\approx1.4287$ (about $42.87\%$ net growth). Exact GDP-per-capita growth is $1.04/1.018-1\approx0.0216$, while a continuous neighbour with force $0.015$ has effective annual rate $e^{0.015}-1\approx0.01511$.

math.title: Carpentry workshop: revenue, cost, and build time
math.context:
A small carpentry workshop builds and sells wooden chairs. Let $Q$ be the number of chairs (treated as continuous). Revenue in euros is $R(Q)=-3Q^{2}+90Q$. Production cost in euros is $C(Q)=0.5Q^{3}-9Q^{2}+60Q+200$. After an assembly-bench reconfiguration the build-time function (hours) is
$$T(Q)=\begin{cases}0.5Q^{2}+4Q & \text{if }Q<12\\ 12Q-24 & \text{if }Q\ge 12.\end{cases}$$
The owner is comparing operating decisions, average-cost movements, and a nearby rival rather than looking at any one formula in isolation. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
statements: Profit (revenue minus cost) reaches its highest value when $Q=15$ chairs are made and sold.
Starting from an output of $Q_{0}$ chairs, building one extra chair changes the average cost per chair by roughly $Q_{0}-9-\dfrac{200}{Q_{0}^{2}}$.
The build-time function $T(Q)$ rises more steeply at $Q=11$ than at $Q=15$.

A rival workshop's revenue $R_{e}(Q)$ satisfies $R_{e}(6)=R(6)$, and its marginal revenue exceeds this workshop's, $R_{e}^{\prime}(Q)>R^{\prime}(Q)$, throughout $6\le Q\le 10$. It then follows that $R_{e}(9)<R(9)$.
Revenue is largest at an output exceeding $12$ chairs.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Profit is revenue minus cost. An interior peak requires $P^{\prime}=0$ with the right sign pattern — guessing $Q=15$ from the revenue schedule is the trap here.

Profit is revenue minus cost, so form $P=R-C$ and look for where its derivative vanishes.

$$
P(Q) = -0.5Q^{3}+6Q^{2}+30Q-200
$$

$$
P^{\prime}(Q) = -1.5Q^{2}+12Q+30
$$

Factoring gives

$$
P^{\prime}(Q) = -1.5(Q-10)(Q+2)
$$

The only positive critical point is $Q=10$, and at $Q=15$ one already has $P^{\prime}(15)<0$, so profit is falling there rather than peaking.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

The one-unit change in average cost is the derivative of $AC=C/Q$, not the derivative of total cost. Divide first, then differentiate.

Average cost is total cost per chair, so divide $C$ by $Q$ before differentiating.

$$
AC(Q) = \dfrac{C(Q)}{Q} = 0.5Q^{2}-9Q+60+\dfrac{200}{Q}
$$

$$
AC^{\prime}(Q) = Q-9-\dfrac{200}{Q^{2}}
$$

Starting from output $Q_{0}$, the change in average cost from one extra chair is approximated by that derivative evaluated at $Q_{0}$, which is exactly the expression in the claim.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Steepness means the local slope $T^{\prime}$ on the active branch. The kink at $Q=12$ forces different formulas at $Q=11$ and $Q=15$.

Steepness of build time is the derivative of whichever branch is active at the stated output.

On $Q<12$,

$$
T^{\prime}(Q) = Q+4
$$

$$
T^{\prime}(11) = 15
$$

On $Q\ge 12$,

$$
T^{\prime}(Q) = 12
$$

$$
T^{\prime}(15) = 12
$$

Since $15>12$, build time rises more steeply at $Q=11$ than at $Q=15$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Equal starting revenue plus a strict marginal-revenue advantage integrates to a larger ending revenue. The claim asserts the opposite inequality.

The rival starts at the same revenue at $Q=6$ but has strictly larger marginal revenue on the way to $Q=9$, so integrate that inequality.

$$
R_{e}(9)-R_{e}(6)>R(9)-R(6)
$$

With $R_{e}(6)=R(6)$, this forces

$$
R_{e}(9)>R(9)
$$

The claim asserts the opposite inequality.

$$
R_{e}(6) = R(6)
$$

$$
Q = 6
$$

$$
Q = 9
$$

which does not match the claim.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Revenue peaks where $R^{\prime}=0$ and $R^{\prime\prime}<0$ — a different first-order condition from the profit peak at $Q=10$.

Revenue peaks where marginal revenue is zero and the second derivative is negative.

$$
R^{\prime}(Q) = -6Q+90 = 0 \implies Q = 15
$$

$$
R^{\prime\prime}(Q) = -6<0
$$

That critical output $15$ exceeds $12$, so revenue is largest beyond twelve chairs.

So the statement is True.
math.solution_overview:
Revenue is $R(Q)=-3Q^{2}+90Q$ and cost is $C(Q)=0.5Q^{3}-9Q^{2}+60Q+200$. Profit $P=R-C$ expands to

$$P(Q)=-0.5Q^{3}+6Q^{2}+30Q-200$$

$$
P^{\prime}(Q) = -1.5Q^{2}+12Q+30 = -1.5(Q-10)(Q+2)
$$

so the only positive critical point is $Q=10$. Marginal revenue is

$$R^{\prime}(Q)=-6Q+90$$

which vanishes at $Q=15$, and $R^{\prime\prime}=-6<0$, so revenue peaks there. Average cost is

$$AC(Q)=0.5Q^{2}-9Q+60+\dfrac{200}{Q}$$

$$AC^{\prime}(Q)=Q-9-\dfrac{200}{Q^{2}}$$

Build time has one-sided slopes $T^{\prime}(Q)=Q+4$ on $Q<12$ and $T^{\prime}(Q)=12$ on $Q\ge 12$. If a rival matches revenue at an endpoint but has strictly larger marginal revenue on an interval, integrating that inequality forces a larger rival revenue at the far end.

math.title: Mildew Across Four Vineyard Blocks
math.context: A family-run vineyard is laid out across four distinct blocks that climb a gentle hillside: Block A on the lower slope, Block B at mid-slope, Block C on the upper slope where the sun exposure is most intense, and Block D on the flat valley floor near a small creek. The vineyard's longtime manager, who has kept meticulous planting records since first taking over the property, reports that the blocks are not equal in size: for every 3 rows of vines in Block D, there are 4 rows in Block A, 6 rows in Block B, and 7 rows in Block C. This season, an outbreak of powdery mildew — a fungal disease that thrives in specific combinations of humidity and sun exposure — has prompted the manager to inspect a sample of rows from each block and record infection counts, separate from the routine pest-monitoring the vineyard also performs for an unrelated insect species. In Block A, inspectors found mildew in 8 of the 200 rows examined. In Block B, 27 of 300 rows examined showed signs of mildew. Block C, with its intense upper-slope sun exposure, had the highest infection count: 70 of 350 rows examined. Block D, nearest the creek and therefore more humid, still showed a meaningful rate: 21 of 150 rows examined. During today's inspection round, a randomly selected row is found to show clear signs of powdery mildew. ● (a) Find the probability that this infected row is in Block C. ● (b) Suppose the vineyard manager later confirms — from the row's marker tag — that this infected row is definitely NOT in Block C. Given both this and the fact that it is infected, find the probability that the row is in Block B.
statements: The probability that a row shows mildew is greater than 10%.
The probability that the row is in Block C AND shows mildew equals 7%.
The probability that the row is in Block C, given it shows mildew is greater than 60%.
The probability that a row shows no mildew equals 1 minus the probability that a row shows mildew.
The probability that the row is in Block B, given it shows mildew AND is known not to be in Block C is greater than 45%.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The probability of a randomly selected row showing mildew is $P(M)$. This was calculated using the Law of Total Probability in the overview.

$$
P(M) = 0.126
$$

To compare with the claim, we express this as a percentage:

$$
0.126 = 12.6\%
$$

.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The probability that a row is in Block C and shows mildew is the joint probability $P(C \cap M)$. This is found by multiplying the prior probability of being in Block C by the conditional probability of showing mildew given it's in Block C, $P(M \mid C)$.

$$
P(C \cap M) = P(C) \times P(M \mid C)
$$

Using the values from the overview, $P(C) = 0.35$ and $P(M \mid C) = 0.20$.

$$
P(C \cap M) = 0.35 \times 0.20
$$

$$
0.35 \times 0.2 = 0.07
$$

$$
P(C \cap M) = 0.07
$$

This is exactly $7\%$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The probability that the row is in Block C, given it shows mildew, is the conditional probability $P(C \mid M)$. We apply the definition of conditional probability:

$$
P(C \mid M) = \frac{P(C \cap M)}{P(M)}
$$

From the overview, $P(C \cap M) = 0.070$ and $P(M) = 0.126$.

$$
P(C \mid M) = \frac{0.070}{0.126}
$$

$$
P(C \mid M) \approx 0.5556
$$

Expressed as a percentage, this is approximately $55.56\%$. The claim states this probability is greater than $60\%$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The event that a row shows no mildew is the complement of the event that a row shows mildew. Let $M^c$ be the event that a row shows no mildew. For any event $E$, the probability of its complement $E^c$ is given by $P(E^c) = 1 - P(E)$.

Therefore, the probability of a row showing no mildew is $P(M^c) = 1 - P(M)$. This matches the formula given in the claim.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The probability of the row being in Block B, given it shows mildew AND is known not to be in Block C, can be written as $P(B \mid M \cap C^c)$. Let $C^c$ be the event that the row is not in Block C. By definition of conditional probability:

$$
P(B \mid M \cap C^c) = \frac{P(B \cap M \cap C^c)}{P(M \cap C^c)}
$$

If a row is in Block B, it cannot also be in Block C. Thus, the event $B \cap C^c$ is simply the event $B$. So, the numerator $P(B \cap M \cap C^c)$ simplifies to $P(B \cap M)$. From the overview, $P(B \cap M) = 0.027$.

The denominator $P(M \cap C^c)$ represents the probability that a row shows mildew and is not in Block C. This is the sum of the joint probabilities of mildew occurring in Blocks A, B, and D:

$$
P(M \cap C^c) = P(A \cap M) + P(B \cap M) + P(D \cap M)
$$

Using the joint probabilities from the overview:

$$
P(M \cap C^c) = 0.008 + 0.027 + 0.021
$$

$$
0.008 + 0.027 = 0.035
$$

$$
0.035 + 0.021 = 0.056
$$

$$
P(M \cap C^c) = 0.056
$$

Now we compute the conditional probability:

$$
P(B \mid M \cap C^c) = \frac{0.027}{0.056}
$$

$$
P(B \mid M \cap C^c) \approx 0.4821
$$

Expressed as a percentage, this is approximately $48.21\%$.

So the statement is True.
math.solution_overview:
This problem describes a vineyard with four blocks (A, B, C, D), each with a specific proportion of the total rows and a distinct rate of powdery mildew infection. We are given relative block sizes and observed infection rates from samples within each block. A row is randomly selected and found to be infected, and we must evaluate various probabilities related to this event.

First, we establish the prior probabilities for a randomly chosen row belonging to each block. The problem states that for every 3 rows in Block D, there are 4 rows in Block A, 6 rows in Block B, and 7 rows in Block C. The total number of relative parts is $4+6+7+3 = 20$. Let $A, B, C, D$ denote the events that a row is from the respective block.

$$
P(A) = \frac{4}{20} = 0.20
$$
$$
P(B) = \frac{6}{20} = 0.30
$$
$$
P(C) = \frac{7}{20} = 0.35
$$
$$
P(D) = \frac{3}{20} = 0.15
$$

Next, we calculate the conditional probabilities of a row showing mildew, given its block. Let $M$ denote the event that a row shows mildew. These are derived from the sample data provided for each block.

$P(M \mid A) = \frac{8}{200} = 0.04$
$P(M \mid B) = \frac{27}{300} = 0.09$
$P(M \mid C) = \frac{70}{350} = 0.20$
$P(M \mid D) = \frac{21}{150} = 0.14$

To find the overall probability of a randomly selected row showing mildew, $P(M)$, we apply the Law of Total Probability, summing the joint probabilities for each block:

$$P(M) = P(M \mid A)P(A) + P(M \mid B)P(B) + P(M \mid C)P(C) + P(M \mid D)P(D)$$

$$P(M) = (0.04)(0.20) + (0.09)(0.30) + (0.20)(0.35) + (0.14)(0.15)$$
$$P(M) = 0.008 + 0.027 + 0.070 + 0.021$$
$$P(M) = 0.126$$

The joint probabilities for a row being in a specific block and showing mildew are:

$$
P(A \cap M) = P(M \mid A)P(A) = 0.008
$$
$$
P(B \cap M) = P(M \mid B)P(B) = 0.027
$$
$$
P(C \cap M) = P(M \mid C)P(C) = 0.070
$$
$$
P(D \cap M) = P(M \mid D)P(D) = 0.021
$$

Note that the sum of these joint probabilities equals $P(M)$: $0.008 + 0.027 + 0.070 + 0.021 = 0.126$.

math.title: Community Clinic Screening
math.context: On a screening day with 80 independent patients, positives and negatives are expected in the ratio 3 : 17. The standard deviation of the number of positives that day is $\sqrt{10.2}$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: A given patient screens negative with probability 0.85.
Among the next 20 patients, the expected number of positive screens is 4.
For 40 patients, the variance of the number of positive screens is 5.1.
The probability of 3 consecutive positive screens is less than 0.005.
The probability of at most 1 positive screen among the next 8 patients is more than 0.7.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

From the stem quantities, recover the common success probability step by step.

$$
p = \dfrac{3}{3+17} = 0.15
$$

Each independent trial either succeeds or fails, so the failure probability is the complement

$$
1-p
$$

Substituting the recovered value,

$$
1-p = 1-0.15
$$

$$
1 - 0.15 = 0.85
$$

This agrees with the probability stated in the claim.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

For a binomial count $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, the mean is the product of the number of trials and the success probability:

$$
E[X] = np
$$

Using $n=20$ and the recovered $p=0.15$,

$$
E[X] = 20\cdot 0.15
$$

$$
20 \times 0.15 = 3
$$

The claim reports $4$, which is not equal to the computed mean $3$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

For $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, the variance formula is

$$
\mathrm{Var}(X) = np(1-p)
$$

Insert $n=40$, $p=0.15$, and $1-p=0.85$:

$$
\mathrm{Var}(X) = 40\cdot 0.15\cdot 0.85
$$

$$
40 \times 0.15 = 6
$$

$$
6 \times 0.85 = 5.1
$$

This matches the variance stated in the claim.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Independence across trials means a run of successes multiplies the same probability $p$ on every trial:

$$
P(\text{3 successes in a row}) = p^{3}
$$

With the recovered $p=0.15$,

$$
p^{3} = (0.15)^{3}
$$

$$
0.0034
$$

Compare with the claimed cutoff $0.005$:

$$
0.0034 < 0.005
$$

The inequality in the claim therefore holds.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Let $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(8,0.15)$. The event “at most $1$ successes” is the union of the mutually exclusive outcomes $X=0,1,\ldots,1$, so

$$
P(X\le 1) = \sum_{x = 0}^{1} \binom{8}{x}p^{x}(1-p)^{8-x}
$$

Evaluating each mass separately:

$$
P(X = 0) = \binom{8}{0}(0.15)^{0}(0.85)^{8}\approx 0.2725
$$

$$
\binom{8}{0} = 1
$$

$$
P(X = 1) = \binom{8}{1}(0.15)^{1}(0.85)^{7}\approx 0.3847
$$

Adding these contributions,

$$
P(X\le 1)
$$

$$
0.6572
$$

Compared with $0.7$, we obtain $0.6572 \le 0.7$. The claim's inequality does not hold.

So the statement is False.
math.solution_overview:
On a screening day with 80 independent patients, positives and negatives are expected in the ratio 3 : 17. The standard deviation of the number of positives that day is $\sqrt{10.2}$.

Successes and failures are expected in the ratio $3:17$, so

$$
p = \dfrac{3}{3+17} = 0.15
$$

We model the count as $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(80,0.15)$.
